content.text: Refreshing only the rows that changed

inlineContent.text: re-reads every row of every registered entity. When something already told you
identities changed — a sync signal, a server push, a screen that knows what it just touched —
spends that knowledge instead of rediscovering it:

code: await persistence.mergeRemote(into: store, ids: changedIDs, deleted: tombstonedIDs)

inlineContent.text: One batched fetch per 500 IDs instead of a full-table scan, and only the named entities are reconciled — everything else in state is left exactly as it was. Every guarantee
makes still holds: pending writes flush first, and an ID with unflushed local intent always wins.
The one difference is deletions. A partial read can’t tell a deleted row from one you simply didn’t ask about, so this
infers a deletion — an ID vanishes only if you name it in
, and only if the resolved policy allows removal. Name only what you have positive evidence for. In exchange there’s no empty-snapshot guard to work around, so unlike
hold defers is remembered and re-offered on the next call, on top of whatever you name in
. You don’t have to re-queue the ID yourself, which matters because the signal that named it is usually spent — so a hold delays a remote change here rather than vetoing it.
shares the same debt, so either path delivers what the other deferred.

SwiftData records a transaction log for every file-backed store, whether or not you read it.
is what reads it; nothing else trims it, so left alone it grows for the life of the app.
So the coordinator prunes it — transactions older than

For exports, migrations, diagnostics, or any other “what’s actually on disk?” question, read directly — naming your domain type, not its generated shadow:

inlineContent.text: Both flush the debounce window first by default, so they can’t return a stale row for something the user just edited; pass
on a hot path where that doesn’t matter. Both report failures to
rethrow — there is no state to leave untouched here, so swallowing the error could only present an unreadable database as “no data”.
The entity does not have to be registered with the coordinator; reading a model that is in the container’s schema but not mirrored into state is fine.

Every save and fetch failure is logged, and the coordinator accepts an optional
handler to additionally surface it to your app (a failed
untouched rather than presenting an unreadable store as “no data”):

code: guard failure.isFinal else { return }   // earlier attempts may still succeed
// e.g. dispatch an action that shows a "couldn't save" banner

inlineContent.text: A flush clears its buffers before the save runs, so a save that fails has nothing left to retry it — the write would reach disk only if the user happened to touch the same entity again. That is silent data loss, so the stack retries.
into the writer’s pending buffers, never over anything newer: a later edit to the same entity supersedes the restored value, and a deletion drained while the save was in flight cancels it.
then re-attempts on a doubling backoff, independently of the debounce timer — a write has to land even if the user never touches the app again.
Retrying is bounded, because a write that can
succeed (disk full, a model the container can’t encode) must not keep the stack busy forever. Tune it with
is that policy — five attempts over roughly seven seconds.
opts out of retrying without opting back into losing the write.
